Scale and coordination demands increase →
Emergency Operations Center (EOC)

“A centralized physical or virtual location where government agencies, organizations, and key decision makers gather to coordinate overall disaster response and recovery.”

FEMA, 2022
FEMA (2022). EOC Quick Reference Guide.3
Background

Intro to an EOC

01Two levels

EOCs exist at both the county and state (sEOC) levels.

02Few, if any, employees

EOCs ‘borrow’ employees from other agencies when activated.

03Ad hoc teams

Employees represent their ‘home’ agency and form teams that may have never worked together before.

04Activation depends on local regulations

Can include emergencies that exceed “normal resources” or need multiple agencies, emergency declarations, and ongoing hazards.

FEMA (2022).4

Gap

Existing measures to study an EOC

Generic teamwork features

Based on general teamwork (e.g., TeamSTEPPS) rather than context-dependent, interorganizational features.

Taylor, 2011; Morian et al., 2023
Observational research is equally limited
  • Requires multiple researchers, often rotating
  • After-action reviews
  • Observer-rated behavioral checklists
EOC-generated materials

Provide little insight into the how or why.

7
Gap

Existing methodologies emphasize qualitative and subjective data

Useful to capture preferences, but missing a team science perspective. Neal, 2003

In large teams
SMMShared mental models
SASituation awareness
TCTeam cognition
TMSTransactive memory systems
↓ Strong empirical links to team performance, coordination, and adaptability Mathieu et al., 2000
Insufficient shared understanding can show up as
Communication inefficienciesUneven participationDelayed coordination
Mathieu et al., 2000
In an EOC, SMMs may
Facilitate interagency coordinationBuild effective TMSCreate resilient teams
Kapucu, 2006; Cooke et al., 2000
Thus, there is a need to study the underlying mechanisms of large-scale teams in an EOC.

Aims

Aims and objectives

Build on existing methodologies by combining subjective and objective measurements to quantify situation awareness, mental models, and coordination.

Subjective

Post-exercise survey of workers’ beliefs and preferences

Method

The sEOC

3
GoPro cameras
  • 1080p, ~90% of the sEOC
  • Left and right on 400 cm tripods; middle on 130 cm tripod
  • Continuous recording, saved in hour-long segments
10
Sony voice recorders
  • Placed around the room
  • 2 at tables where high communication was expected

Results · Survey (n = 17)

Subjective results

Situation awareness is the gapLow awareness of other teams’ tasks (M = 2.41)
Movement drives coordinationWorkers walk over rather than rely on seating (M = 4.65)
No one-size-fits-all workstationResponses vary widely by workstation
Procedures need monitoringRoom to track familiarity with responsibilities
Cross-team situation awareness, not workstation comfort, as the main design target
Mean ± SD agreement by item, 1 = strongly disagree, 5 = strongly agree.16

Discussion

Discussion

Prior workThis work
Self-report and observation miss proximity, movement, positioningDubrow & Bannan, 2019
→
Video tracking of movement and positioning, no observers
Wearable proximity sensors on every participantOzella et al., 2019
→
No added equipment or burden on responders during operations
Centralized communication as a source of leader overloadYuan & van Knippenberg, 2022
→
One speaker carries ~50% of speech; centrality as a real-time overload flag
Understanding EOC inner workings is time-intensiveMoon et al., 2018
→
Regions of interest point designers to congestion and coordination hotspots
Dubrow & Bannan, 2019; Ozella et al., 2019; Yuan & van Knippenberg, 2022; Moon et al., 201820
Discussion

Limitations

Validation
  • No full manual validation yet; only part of processed video reviewed
Video
  • ID switching persists across the EOC, worst for people far from the camera
  • ID switching blocks individual-level behavioral analysis
Audio
  • Coverage limited by recorder placement and number
  • Diarization drift as speakers leave and join tables
  • Pickup from neighboring tables; speaker ID inconsistencies, similar to video
21
Conclusions

Unobtrusive multimodal measures surface sEOC human factors issues

Cross-team situation awareness

Low awareness of other teams (M = 2.41) despite highly connected speakers within teams (0.87)

Movement as coordination

Workers walk over to talk (M = 4.65); video captures movement without observers or wearables

Concentrated communication load

Top speaker carries 50% of group speech; centrality as a leader-overload signal

NEXT STEPS
→Support for cross-team information sharing
→Movement hotspots linked to layout redesign
→Real-time centrality to flag leader overload
→Video tracking validated against manual review
